strengths: Clear problem identification with strong empirical motivation: toy experiments (Fig. 2) effectively demonstrate why sparse attention fails on AR models and motivate the proposed solution
Theoretically grounded approach: connects sparsity-induced error to noise levels and denoising steps, providing intuition for chunk-aware sparsity allocation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: tested on two AR models (Self-Forcing, LongLive), extensive VBench evaluation across 16 dimensions, thorough ablation studies, and careful baseline adaptation
Strong practical results: achieves 19.7 FPS on consumer GPU (RTX 5090), even surpasses dense attention in total score (84.5 vs 84.1), demonstrating dense attention redundancy
Well-designed complementary components: CAG allocates sparsity based on error accumulation while HSA performs hierarchical selection—both address specific limitations of naive sparse attention
Excellent presentation: clear writing, well-designed figures (Fig. 3, 5), logical flow from motivation to solution, good qualitative examples
weaknesses: Loose theoretical-practice connection: the jump from theoretical TV bound (Eq. 4) to specific sparsity allocation formula (Eq. 5) lacks rigorous derivation; how α_i is computed in practice and verified to follow 1/√t scaling is unclear

Limited experimental scope: only 1.3B models evaluated (generalization to 7B/14B uncertain), only 5-second videos (error accumulation dynamics on longer sequences unknown), no statistical significance testing (missing error bars/confidence intervals)

CAG mechanism concerns: no ablation on hyperparameters s_target and s_base, Table 2 shows CAG alone degrades Dynamic Degree metric (37.5 vs 63.1), suggesting CAG can harm important metrics and its interaction with HSA is underexplored

HSA design choices lack full justification: why mean pooling over alternatives? Why must current chunk always use dense attention? Sensitivity analysis only tests narrow topk range {6,9,12}; claimed 2% frame-retrieval overhead lacks detailed breakdown

Marginal improvements over dense attention: main result is +0.4% on total score (84.5 vs 84.1), speedup of 1.3× is useful but not dramatic; some metrics show trade-offs (e.g., Dynamic Degree varies across models)

Theory-practice gap: theoretical analysis (Appendix B) applies to individual chunks independently without accounting for error compounding across chunks; theory doesn't explain why the specific formula is chosen over alternatives

Incomplete comparisons: only compared against sparse attention methods, not other efficiency techniques (linear attention, low-rank variants); baseline adaptation necessary makes it harder to isolate contribution; no comparison with simpler alternatives

Reproducibility limitations: code not yet released, post-training requires 2,000 iterations (limited accessibility), hyperparameter selection process not described, resolution adjustment rationale unclear
Narrow evaluation scope: only tested on few AR models and 5-second videos; no failure case analysis or discussion of which video types the method struggles with; cherry-picked qualitative examples

Technical details underexplored: asymmetric compression (k̂^{<i} compressed but within-chunk keys not) lacks justification; which complex attention patterns (Fig. 4) HSA actually captures versus misses is unclear

strengths: Clearly motivates the problem with Figure 1 showing attention dominates latency in AR video generation (~75%)
Novel observation that early-chunk sparsity causes irreversible degradation while late-chunk sparsity is tolerable, specific to AR models (Figure 2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two AR models (Self Forcing, LongLive) with five baseline methods
Strong empirical results: achieves 84.5 VBench score exceeding dense attention (84.1) and 19.7 FPS on consumer GPU
Includes ablation studies (Tables 2-3) demonstrating component contributions and robustness to hyperparameter choices
Practical end-to-end speedup (1.3×) addresses real deployment constraint
weaknesses: Theoretical justification is disconnected from the method: Equation 4 (TV bound) does not analyze sparse attention effects—sparsity never appears in Appendix B's proof. The connection between the TV bound and linear sparsity allocation (Eq 5-6) is tenuous.
Equation 6's FLOPs-balancing constraint is arbitrary and unjustified. Why optimize equal FLOPs rather than quality subject to latency budget? No ablation on this design choice.
Limited to 1.3B models only, contradicting claims of enabling 'real-time generation for the first time.' Generalization to larger model scales (7B+) is unknown and critical for 2026 standards.

Experimental fairness issues: (1) Resolution adjusted from 480×832 to 512×768 to 'avoid padding,' preventing fair comparison; (2) Different inference backends used (SpargeAttention vs FlashInfer); (3) Baseline fine-tuning status not clearly marked.

CAG mechanism relies on anecdotal proof: Figure 2 shows only 7 chunks with 3 sparsity levels. The claim that α_i ∝ 1/√t is stated without derivation. No systematic study of longer videos (only 5 seconds).

HSA design under-motivated: mean pooling (Eq 7) is simplistic with no ablation; fixed top-k contradicts Figure 4 showing attention patterns vary across layers/heads/timesteps; coarse-to-fine strategy never empirically compared against alternatives.

Ablation study reveals concerning trade-offs not explained: +CAG increases Aesthetic Quality but drops Dynamic Degree (46.4→37.5 in Table 2), a regression left unanalyzed. No clear mechanistic understanding of component interactions.

Severe reproducibility concerns: (1) Code not provided; (2) Noise level α_i estimation method unspecified; (3) Top-k frame selection metric not detailed; (4) Fine-tuning hyperparameters (learning rate, schedule) for 2,000 steps omitted.

Hyperparameter selection unexplained: s_target=0.9, s_base=0.98 lack justification. Unlike Table 3's sensitivity analysis for top-k, no ablation on s_base across model scales. Generalization of these values unknown.

Limited novelty: adapting existing sparse attention methods to AR video generation with chunk-aware modifications is intuitive but incremental. Primarily an engineering contribution without new algorithmic or theoretical insights.

Generalization unknown: only tested on Self Forcing and LongLive; transfer to other AR architectures (CausVid, Magi-1, SkyReels-V2, etc.) not evaluated. Fixed chunk size of 3 frames; behavior on other chunk sizes unexplored.
19.7 FPS claim depends on orthogonal techniques (LightVAE, FP8 quantization) beyond the proposed method, inflating the practical impact attribution.
No failure mode analysis: Figure 5 shows only success cases. When does LIGHT FORCING degrade? Are there prompts/scenes with worse sparse-attention tolerance?

strengths: First sparse attention solution specifically designed for autoregressive video generation models, addressing a well-identified problem where existing methods fail (demonstrated clearly in Section 4.1)
Novel chunk-aware growth mechanism with theoretical grounding in error analysis, providing principled sparsity allocation across chunks based on accumulation errors
Comprehensive experimental validation including multiple models (Self Forcing, LongLive), extensive baseline comparisons, detailed ablation studies, and sensitivity analysis
Practical impact: achieves real-time video generation (19.7 FPS) on consumer GPUs for the first time, with clear potential applications
Well-designed hierarchical sparse attention using coarse-to-fine frame and block selection, effectively mitigating long-range consistency issues
Honest discussion of limitations and good reproducibility with detailed implementation specifications, hyperparameter documentation, and promised code release
Clear presentation with effective use of visualizations (Figure 2's toy experiments, Figure 4's attention patterns) and well-structured writing
weaknesses: Marginal empirical improvements over dense attention (0.4-0.7 points on VBench), which may be within noise margins for generative models and questions the practical significance despite added complexity

Significant theory-practice gap: the connection between the TV error bound (Eq. 4) and concrete sparsity formula (Eq. 5) is abrupt; logarithmic factors are dismissed without discussing their practical magnitude
Limited experimental scope: only 1.3B models evaluated; scaling to larger models (14B) is unclear despite being important for 2026; single benchmark (VBench) with no cross-dataset validation
Modest end-to-end speedup (1.3×) given aggressive sparsity ratios (80-90%), raising questions about practical value relative to implementation complexity

Incomplete ablations: no justification for keeping first chunk dense or exploration of HSA design choices beyond top-k parameter; missing sensitivity analysis on core hyperparameters (s_base, s_target)

Fair comparison concerns: different baselines use different sparsity ratios; VMoBA's poor LongLive performance suggests potential tuning issues; method requires post-training while some baselines don't
Missing critical implementation details: exact computation of αᵢ in practice, precise connection to noise levels σₜ, convergence analysis for post-training procedure

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First sparse attention solution specifically designed for AR video generation models, with well-motivated observation that error accumulation differs fundamentally from bidirectional models
Theoretically grounded CAG mechanism: Error analysis in Appendix C provides principled justification for progressive sparsity allocation based on sampling and score estimation errors

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple models (Self Forcing, LongLive, InfiniteForcing), benchmarks (VBench, VBench-Long), thorough ablations, and qualitative comparisons demonstrating superiority
Strong empirical results: Achieves 1.3× speedup while matching or exceeding dense attention quality (84.5 vs 84.1 on Self Forcing); enables real-time generation (27.4 FPS on consumer GPUs)
Convincing motivation via toy experiments: Figure 2 effectively demonstrates quality degradation patterns across chunks and justifies the need for chunk-aware sparsity allocation
Thorough reproducibility: Code released, detailed implementation details, hyperparameter specifications, multiple GPU platforms evaluated, comprehensive appendix with proofs and additional ablations

Clear presentation and honest limitations: Well-structured paper with effective visualizations; authors acknowledge model-specific benefits, evaluation limitations (1.3B only), and remaining artifacts
weaknesses: HSA mechanism lacks theoretical justification: Hierarchical attention with mean pooling and top-k selection is primarily heuristic; connection to preserving 'informative context' relies on intuition rather than theoretical grounding

Modest standalone speedups: Primary contribution achieves only 1.2-1.3× speedup from sparse attention alone; significant end-to-end improvements (2-3×) depend heavily on orthogonal optimizations (FP8, kernel fusion, LightVAE), obscuring the method's true contribution
Limited evaluation scope: All experiments restricted to 1.3B models; scaling to larger models (7B-14B) remains unexplored and critical for understanding generalizability

Model-dependent and variable improvements: Gains decrease across tested models (Self Forcing 84.5→84.1, LongLive 83.9→83.2); some metrics degrade significantly with CAG alone (Dynamic Degree 84.2→66.7)

Incomplete empirical validation of core assumptions: Proportionality αᵢ ∝ 1/√T is derived theoretically but not validated empirically; connection between actual noise levels in trained models and this relationship remains assumed

Complex hyperparameter tuning required: Duration-specific settings (Table 5) with no clear guidance; sensitivity analysis limited to three topk values; fine-tuning overhead (2,000 iterations) not fully accounted in efficiency claims
HSA overhead undercharacterized: Claimed 2% frame-retrieval overhead is rough estimate not rigorously measured across varying history lengths, block sizes, or hardware platforms
Artifacts not fully resolved: Authors acknowledge white band-like artifacts persist in some samples (Figures 8-9), only alleviated by HSA, suggesting approach lacks full robustness

Incomplete computational analysis: Total cost of frame selection (Eq. 8-9) plus blockwise pooling (Eq. 7) not formally analyzed; claim of 'fixed attention complexity' only applies post-frame-selection

Peak memory unchanged: Table 11 shows sparse attention alone provides no memory benefits; improvements require additional optimizations, limiting the method's standalone utility for memory-constrained devices

strengths: Well-motivated observation that existing sparse attention methods fail for AR models due to error accumulation; toy experiments in Figure 2 effectively demonstrate the problem
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple AR models (Self Forcing, LongLive, InfiniteForcing) and benchmarks (VBench, VBench-Long) with multiple metrics
Practical achievement of real-time video generation (27.4 FPS on RTX 5090) with generalization across multiple AR models
Solid ablation studies demonstrating necessity of both CAG and HSA components, with robustness analysis of hyperparameters
Achieves parity or improvement over dense attention (84.5 vs 84.1 Total Score), suggesting effective compression of attention redundancy
Extensive supplementary materials with detailed implementation, hyperparameters, and additional experiments supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Weak theoretical justification: the connection between the variance distance bound (Eq. 4) and sparsity-induced error is not rigorously established. The claim that αᵢ ∝ 1/√T is stated but not formally derived for the sparse attention case, and why the linear formula in Eq. (5) is optimal is never proven

Arbitrary design choices lacking principled justification: the FLOP-equality constraint (Eq. 6) is pragmatic but not theoretically motivated; s_base varies across scenarios (0.98 vs 0.95), suggesting ad-hoc tuning; HSA's frame-then-block hierarchy and always-selected frame set choices appear intuitive but lack formal derivation

Disproportionate speedup given sparsity level: achieving only 1.3× attention speedup with ~80-90% sparsity suggests significant overhead or suboptimal design. Modern sparse kernels typically achieve 2-3× speedup at such high sparsity ratios. The impressive 3.08× end-to-end number depends heavily on orthogonal optimizations (FP8, kernels, LightVAE); core sparse attention contributes only ~1.3×

Limited experimental scope: only 1.3B models evaluated (below 2026 standards); only 3 similar recent AR models tested; no evaluation of quality-efficiency tradeoff across different sparsity levels; no characterization of failure modes beyond mentioning 'subtle artifacts may remain'

Experimental setup fairness concerns: baseline methods finetuned for only 2000 iterations which may be insufficient; LIGHT FORCING has carefully tuned hyperparameters (Table 5) while baselines use fixed ratios, potentially giving unfair advantage; resolution normalization choice benefits some methods more than others

Limited technical novelty: importance-based sparsity allocation and hierarchical attention are well-established techniques in pruning and language model literature. The AR-specific focus is novel but individual components are incremental

Incomplete analysis of practical applicability: peak memory unchanged with sparse attention alone; method tightly coupled to recent AR models; no investigation of scaling to larger models despite acknowledging this as important direction

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear demonstration that naive sparse attention fails for AR models (Figure 2 toy experiments effectively illustrate quality collapse)

Strong empirical results: achieves 84.5 on VBench (better than dense attention's 84.1), 1.3× attention speedup, 3.08× end-to-end speedup with full optimizations, enabling real-time generation (27.4 FPS on consumer GPU)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three AR models (Self Forcing, LongLive, InfiniteForcing), two benchmarks (VBench, VBench-Long), multiple baselines, and three GPU platforms with detailed ablations
Theoretical grounding for CAG through error analysis (Equation 4) connecting sparsity effects to finite-step sampling error and score estimation error
Clear presentation with good motivation, effective visualizations, and logical flow; detailed implementation details and hyperparameters enable reproducibility with code promised for release
Practical impact: enables real-time AR video generation on consumer hardware through well-thought-out optimization stack (FP8 layers, kernel fusion, efficient VAE)
Honest discussion of limitations (1.3B model scale only, potential artifacts, GPU-specific kernel optimizations) demonstrates scientific integrity
weaknesses: Theoretical justification for CAG is loose: the connection between the error bound (Eq. 4) and sparsity allocation formula (Eq. 5-6) is not rigorously derived; why exactly does error ∝ 1/√T lead to s_i ∝ 1/√T? The enforcement of FLOPs equality (Eq. 6) to solve for β appears somewhat ad-hoc
Limited model diversity: only 1.3B models evaluated; no analysis of scaling to larger models (e.g., 14B) or other AR architectures, limiting generalization claims

Incomplete ablations on HSA design: mean pooling used without comparing alternatives (max, attention-based aggregation); sensitivity analysis limited to topk ∈ {6,9,12} (narrow range); multiple hyperparameters (n_sink, n_win) not thoroughly ablated

Comparison fairness concerns: different baselines tuned to different sparsity ratios (80%-90%); SVG2 shows dramatic latency gap (21.38s vs. 7.39s) raising questions about implementation fidelity; baseline adjustment for AR setting introduces confounds

Failure mode analysis is superficial: white band artifacts in long-video generation acknowledged but not systematically characterized; no metrics quantifying artifact prevalence or analysis of which video types cause issues

HSA overhead claimed at ~2% but not characterized with respect to sequence length scaling; limited comparison to simpler alternatives (sliding window + sparse attention); coarse-to-fine design not validated against other hierarchical approaches
Memory efficiency gains minimal: Table 11 shows peak memory unchanged with sparse attention alone, suggesting limited memory bandwidth improvements despite the focus on attention optimization

Narrow evaluation scope: only tested on recent, similar-architecture AR models; applicability to older architectures or other AR domains (text, audio) unclear; only 3-frame chunks tested without sensitivity analysis
